course.title: Rust Foundations
course.description: Read, run and write small Rust programs, with the real compiler checking your work.
course.audience: Someone new to Rust. Some programming in another language helps but isn't needed.

modules.title: First programs
modules.description: Printing, variables, number types and functions.

concepts.title: Variables and printing
concepts.summary: let names a value and println! prints it. Add mut when the value has to change.

concepts.title: Types and functions
concepts.summary: Whole and decimal number types, and functions that return their last expression.

lessons.title: Print a value, then change it

steps.headline: A Rust program starts at fn main and runs its lines from top to bottom.

lead.text: The code inside fn main() { } runs first. println! prints one line. Each {} in its text is replaced by the next value after the comma.
The ! marks println! as a macro. You call it like a function, but its name always ends in !.
Now write a whole program yourself. Run it as often as you like before you check it.
let gives a value a name. Writing a name inside the braces, as in {area}, prints that variable.

reveal.text: Each let named a value, and later lines used the names. Rust worked out from 6 and 4 that these are whole numbers.

lead.text: This program tries to add 5 to score after creating it. Decide whether rustc accepts it, then run it to see what the compiler says.

reveal.text: A variable made with plain let keeps its first value. Rust makes you say up front which values will change, so a reader knows where to look.

outcome.diagnostics:
error[E0384]: cannot assign twice to immutable variable `score`
 --> main.rs:3:5
  |
2 |     let score = 10;
  |         ----- first assignment to `score`
3 |     score = score + 5;
  |     ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^ cannot assign twice to immutable variable
  |
help: consider making this binding mutable
  |
2 |     let mut score = 10;
  |         +++

error: aborting due to 1 previous error

For more information about this error, try `rustc --explain E0384`.

lead.text: Here is the same program. Make it compile. Run it first and read what rustc suggests.

reveal.text: rustc often tells you the fix. Here it pointed at line 2 and suggested let mut score.

lead.text: A second let with the same name makes a new variable that hides the first. This is called shadowing, and it needs no mut.

reveal.text: Shadowing makes a new variable each time. mut changes the same one. Shadowing also lets the new variable have a different type.

lessons.orientation: Write a program that prints values, and choose which of its variables may change.
lessons.reviewLabel: Print a value, then change it
lessons.nextAction: Give your values types and put a calculation in a function.

blocks.text: Here is a complete Rust program. You haven't learned any Rust yet, but try reading it anyway.

intro.promise: By the end you'll write Rust that prints values, and you'll decide which variables may change.

recap.keyIdea: let names a value, and that value stays fixed unless you write let mut. A second let makes a new variable instead.

blocks.text: You wrote your first two programs and fixed rustc's E0384 error twice: once with mut, once with shadowing.

recap.nextHook: So far Rust guessed every type. Next you'll write the types yourself and put a calculation in a function.

lessons.title: Types and functions

steps.headline: Every value has a type: i32 for whole numbers, f64 for numbers with a decimal point.

lead.text: Rust works out the type from the value. 7 is an i32, a 32-bit integer, and 7.0 is an f64. Dividing two i32 values drops the remainder. Dividing two f64 values keeps it.
You can write a type yourself after a colon, as in let price: f64 = 2.5. Rust never converts between number types on its own. Does this compile?

reveal.text: Write price * count as f64 to convert count first. as converts one number type into another, and you choose where it happens.

outcome.diagnostics:
error[E0277]: cannot multiply `f64` by `i32`
 --> main.rs:4:26
  |
4 |     println!("{}", price * count);
  |                          ^ no implementation for `f64 * i32`
  |
  = help: the trait `Mul<i32>` is not implemented for `f64`
help: the following other types implement trait `Mul<Rhs>`
 --> /rustc/01f6ddf7588f42ae2d7eb0a2f21d44e8e96674cf/library/core/src/ops/arith.rs:361:1
  |
  = note: `&f64` implements `Mul<f64>`
  |
  = note: `&f64` implements `Mul`
  |
  = note: `f64` implements `Mul<&f64>`
  |
  = note: `f64` implements `Mul`
  = note: this error originates in the macro `mul_impl` (in Nightly builds, run with -Z macro-backtrace for more info)

error: aborting due to 1 previous error

For more information about this error, try `rustc --explain E0277`.

lead.text: as converts one number type into another, as in count as f64. Use it to fix the program you just saw.

steps.headline: A function names a calculation. Its parameters and its return value all have types.

lead.text: fn double(n: i32) -> i32 takes an i32 called n and returns an i32. The type after -> is the return type. The last line of the body, written without a semicolon, is the value the function returns.
Write a function of your own. The checker calls it with several numbers, so it has to work for any i32.
add_tax adds a tenth of the price. main calls it twice and adds the results.

reveal.text: Each call gets its own price. price / 10 is integer division, so add_tax(20) adds 2, not 2.0.

lead.text: This is double again, with one change: a semicolon after n * 2.

reveal.text: A line ending in a semicolon is a statement and produces no value. The body now ends without a value, but the signature promised an i32.

outcome.diagnostics:
error[E0308]: mismatched types
 --> main.rs:1:22
  |
1 | fn double(n: i32) -> i32 {
  |    ------            ^^^ expected `i32`, found `()`
  |    |
  |    implicitly returns `()` as its body has no tail or `return` expression
2 |     n * 2;
  |          - help: remove this semicolon to return this value

error: aborting due to 1 previous error

For more information about this error, try `rustc --explain E0308`.

lead.text: Now the parameters are f64 values. Write the function from its signature and the example.

reveal.text: The brackets add first, then the sum is divided by 2.0. With i32 parameters the same calculation would drop the .5.

lessons.orientation: Choose between whole and decimal numbers, and write functions that take and return typed values.
lessons.nextAction: Write your own programs in the Rust projects.

blocks.text: Seven cookies shared between two people is three and a half each. Here is the same sum in Rust.

intro.promise: By the end you'll write functions with typed parameters and return values, and know when division drops a remainder.

recap.keyIdea: Every value has a type that Rust won't change for you, and a function returns its last expression.

blocks.text: You made 7 / 2 print 3.5, fixed E0277 with as, and wrote functions that the checker called with numbers you never saw.

recap.nextHook: You can now read and fix small programs. The projects ask you to write them.

questions.prompt: What number does this program print?
hints: apples holds 3 and pears holds 4.
The program prints apples + pears.
Add the two values.
questions.onCorrect: 7. You read a Rust program without being told any of its rules.

questions.prompt: Change the program so that it prints 5 and 2.
hints: The braces fill in the order of the values after the text.
Swap the 2 and the 5 after the comma.
questions.onCorrect: The braces take the values in order, so swapping the values swaps the output.

questions.prompt: Write a program that prints two lines: Hello, Rust! and then 3 + 4 = 7. Let Rust work out the 7 by putting 3 + 4 after the text.
hints: Each println! prints one line, so you need two of them.
The second one is println!("3 + 4 = {}", 3 + 4);
questions.onCorrect: Two println! calls, two lines. The {} took the value of 3 + 4.

questions.prompt: What number does the program print after area =?
hints: Find width and height first.
area is width * height.
Multiply 6 by 4.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: area is width * height, which is 6 * 4 = 24.

questions.onCorrect: 24. Each let gave a value a name the later lines could use.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds the two sides. area multiplies them.

questions.prompt: Does this program compile?
hints: Look at how score was created, then at line 3.

acceptedIdeas: No. score was made without mut, so it cannot get a new value.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: No. score was made without mut, so it cannot get a new value.

choices.label: No. score was made without mut, so it cannot get a new value.
No. Every let needs a type such as i32.

questions.onCorrect: rustc stops with error E0384 and suggests the fix itself: let mut score.

misconceptions.feedback: It would print 15 if Rust allowed the change. Line 3 gives score a second value, and score never asked for that.
Rust works out the type from 10, so no type is needed here. The problem is on line 3.

questions.prompt: Fix this program so that it compiles and prints 15. You only need to change one line.
hints: Run it first. rustc's message ends with a suggested fix.
score needs to be allowed to change, which is decided where it is created.
Line 2 becomes let mut score = 10;
questions.onCorrect: let mut score said up front that score will change, so line 3 is allowed.

questions.prompt: Fix this program without using mut: turn each line that changes level into a new let. It should print 7.
hints: Lines 3 and 4 give level a new value, which plain let doesn't allow.
Start each of those two lines with let.
Line 3 becomes let level = level * 3;
questions.onCorrect: Each let made a new level from the one before, without any mut.

questions.prompt: Write a program where count starts at 1 and is doubled three times with count = count * 2. Then print count = 8.
hints: count changes after it is created, so it needs mut.
Print it with println!("count = {count}");

questions.prompt: Which word do you write after let so that a variable can be given a new value later?
hints: It is short for mutable.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: mut: let mut count = 0;

questions.prompt: Does let x = 5; followed by let x = "five"; compile?
hints: Is the second line changing x, or making a new one?

acceptedIdeas: Yes. The second let makes a new x, and a new variable can have a new type.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Yes. The second let makes a new x, and a new variable can have a new type.

choices.label: Yes. The second let makes a new x, and a new variable can have a new type.
No. x is an integer, so it can never hold text.
No. You need let mut x for the second line.

misconceptions.feedback: That would be true if line 2 assigned to the same x. A second let makes a new variable.
mut is for assigning to the same variable. A second let does not need it.

questions.prompt: What does this program print?
hints: cookies and people are both whole numbers.
Dividing two whole numbers in Rust gives a whole number.
How many whole times does 2 go into 7?

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 7 / 2 with two whole numbers gives 3. The remainder of 1 is dropped.

questions.onCorrect: 3. Rust divided two whole numbers and dropped the remainder.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the exact answer, but these are whole numbers. Rust keeps the result whole.

questions.prompt: This program prints 3. Change it so that it prints 3.5.
hints: 7 and 2 are i32 values, so the remainder is dropped.
Write both numbers with a decimal point.
questions.onCorrect: 7.0 / 2.0 divides two f64 values, so the .5 is kept.

questions.prompt: Does this program compile?
hints: Look at the two types written after price and count.

acceptedIdeas: No. Rust will not multiply an f64 by an i32 until you convert one of them.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: No. Rust will not multiply an f64 by an i32 until you convert one of them.

choices.label: No. Rust will not multiply an f64 by an i32 until you convert one of them.

questions.onCorrect: rustc reports E0277: cannot multiply f64 by i32. Writing count as f64 fixes it.

misconceptions.feedback: Many languages would do that conversion for you. Rust stops and asks you to choose.
It would, if count were an f64. Rust does not convert it on its own.

questions.prompt: Make this program compile by converting count with as f64. It should print 10.
hints: Only the multiplication needs to change.
Write count as f64 where count is used.
questions.onCorrect: count as f64 turned 4 into 4.0, so both sides of * are f64.

questions.prompt: In fn area(w: i32, h: i32) -> i32, what type does area return?
hints: The return type comes after the arrow.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: i32, the type after the arrow.

questions.onCorrect: i32. The type after -> is what the function hands back.

questions.prompt: Write a function triple that takes an i32 and returns three times it, also as an i32.
hints: The body's last line is the value the function returns.
Write n * 3 with no semicolon after it.
questions.onCorrect: n * 3 with no semicolon is the value triple returns.

questions.prompt: What does this program print?
hints: Work out add_tax(50) and add_tax(20) separately.
price / 10 is integer division: 50 / 10 is 5.
Add 55 and 22.
questions.onCorrect: 77. Each call ran the body with its own price and handed back the last expression.

misconceptions.feedback: That is 50 + 20 without the tax. Each call adds a tenth of its price.

questions.prompt: Does this version compile?
hints: What does a semicolon do to the last line of a function body?

acceptedIdeas: No. The semicolon turns n * 2 into a statement, so the function returns nothing.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: No. The semicolon turns n * 2 into a statement, so the function returns nothing.

choices.label: No. The semicolon turns n * 2 into a statement, so the function returns nothing.
No. A function body must use the word return.

questions.onCorrect: rustc reports E0308 (mismatched types) and suggests removing the semicolon.

misconceptions.feedback: Without the semicolon it would. With it, n * 2 is calculated and thrown away.
return is allowed but not required. The last expression, with no semicolon, is the return value.

questions.prompt: Write a function average that takes two f64 values and returns their average as an f64.
hints: Add the two values, then divide by 2.0.
Brackets make the addition happen first: (a + b) / 2.0
questions.onCorrect: The brackets add before the division, and f64 keeps the fraction.

questions.prompt: Write total_price, which takes a price as an f64 and a count as an i32, and returns price times count as an f64.
hints: count is an i32, so convert it before multiplying.

questions.prompt: Write share, which splits a whole number of sweets between people and returns how many each person gets. Leftover sweets are not shared out.
hints: Dividing two i32 values already drops the remainder.

questions.prompt: Which type does Rust give 2.5 when nothing else in the program says otherwise?
hints: It is a 64-bit floating-point type.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: f64, Rust's default for numbers with a decimal point.

flashcards.front: In Rust, what must you write to give an existing variable a new value with =?
flashcards.back: Create it with let mut, for example let mut count = 0;

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: let mut

flashcards.front: What is it called when a second let reuses a variable's name?
flashcards.back: Shadowing. The new variable hides the old one and may have a different type.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Shadowing

flashcards.front: In Rust, what does 9 / 2 evaluate to?
flashcards.back: 4. Dividing two integers drops the remainder.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 9 / 2 is 4 with remainder 1, which is dropped.

flashcards.front: A Rust function's last line is x + 1; with a semicolon. Why does the function not return x + 1?
flashcards.back: The semicolon makes it a statement. Only a final expression without a semicolon is returned.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The semicolon turns it into a statement.
